title: How I automated strategy research and discovery with AI, without handing my data to anyone (and it does a lot more)
author: OpenTraderWorld
selftext:
For years I coded my strategies in Python and ran them as scripts. I'd get a number at the end, maybe a quick matplotlib chart, and that was it. No real view of what was going on: which setups carried the results, where the drawdowns came from, how a strategy behaved after I changed one parameter three weeks ago. Most of that lived in my head or in files I never reopened.  
  
Today all of that lives in one place, and I drive it with an AI agent. Scheduled workflows pull fresh data and run market scans, and the agent reads my journal, backtests and notes, then updates my research instead of me doing it by hand. It runs on my own machine and doesn't phone home.  
  
How the AI part works: the automator runs workflows on a schedule (imports, scans, reports, daily reviews), and any step can be handed to your own model. There's also a built-in MCP server, so an external agent can read or update modules through token-scoped access. You pick the provider, Anthropic or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so a local model works too. API keys are encrypted at rest and never reach the browser. All of it is off until you turn it on.

  
The backtester has three modes: signal-based, DCA and grid trading. You can load several datasets at once and run the same strategy across them, so it's easy to see where it works and where it falls apart. For indicators, the built-in ones cover the usual stuff, but you can write your own or describe what you have in mind to the agent and let it build it. Either way it shows up on the chart and in the backtester, so you know quickly whether the idea holds up.

  
Then I kept adding the things I was paying for elsewhere, which is the "much more" part:

* Trading journal with fee schedules, multi-currency, and the stats that matter (expectancy, profit factor, R-multiple, drawdown, per-setup performance)
* Historical data downloader that pulls OHLCV from several providers into local datasets, plus charting (candles, Renko, indicators) 
* Rule-based backtester with position sizing and costs 
* Quant tools: VaR, correlation, efficient frontier, Kelly sizing 
* Portfolio tracker, net worth, watchlists, 13F holdings, RSS news, economic calendar 
* Webhooks to pipe alerts in from elsewhere, plus notes, tasks and goals 



Stack is Rust (Axum) + SvelteKit + Postgres, deployed with Docker Compose. No account, no telemetry, and after install it only listens on localhost until you change that. 

What it doesn't do (yet): it doesn't execute or route orders today. 

Right now it's for research, backtesting, journaling and review. 

Trading directly from the app is on the roadmap, more on that below. 

You can get a quick overview of what it does at demo.opentraderworld.com. Since it's public, some features are limited. 

About the license, since the name has "Open" in it: it's not OSI open source. It's FSL-1.1-MIT (Functional Source License). You can use it for free, including commercially at work, modify it, fork it, redistribute it. The only thing you can't do is sell it or run it as a competing paid or hosted service. 

Every release automatically becomes plain MIT two years after it's published. 



What's next: two things are in the pipeline. 

First, a fundamentals module. The default will be free and open data providers, so it works out of the box without spending anything. If you already pay for a provider, you'll be able to plug in your key. The next realease will be public in few days. 

Second, trading from the app. 

The goal is to close the loop: research, backtest, place the trade, and have it land in the journal without copy-pasting anything. 

No date yet, I'd rather ship it right than fast. 

Two real questions for you: 

what fundamentals sources do you actually trust, and which brokers would you want supported first? 

Repo: [github.com/G-OTW/OpenTraderWorld](http://github.com/G-OTW/OpenTraderWorld) 

Site: [opentraderworld.com](http://opentraderworld.com) 

Criticism welcome, especially on the backtester. 

Hope it helps people save time and money.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
Because the MCP agent can update modules and generate custom indicators, I’d make every backtest result reference immutable hashes for the strategy code, indicator code, local OHLCV dataset, and fee schedule. That would let the journal answer your “what changed three weeks ago?” problem without relying on notes or the current module state.

When the same strategy runs across several datasets, does the comparison also record provider-specific adjustments for splits, dividends, delistings, and candle boundaries? A diff showing which trades changed between providers would be especially useful criticism-resistant output.

replies.author: OpenTraderWorld
replies.body:
Yeah, that’s a good point. It’s not the case right now. We do keep the strategy history, so you can still go back and see what a previous run used, but having immutable references for each backtest would be much cleaner. I’ll add that in the next release!   
For the second point, it really depends on the quality of the data provider. Free provider usually means less quality . Better data usually means results that are closer to reality. But yes, comparing providers could also be a good way to show how much bad data can affect a strategy. I’ll work on that too.  
Thanks for the feedback!

comments.author: powerbone
comments.body: Automating MNQ futures backtests is neat, but local AI still overfits static historical data without live execution fees.

replies.author: OpenTraderWorld
replies.body: Well, you can add spread and commissions to the backtest. Spread depends on volatility, so it’s better to use an average.

comments.author: TensorTrader
comments.body: Nice work! Where do you get the data feed from?

replies.author: OpenTraderWorld
replies.body: You will find several data brokers in the app. Some are free, while others require a subscription. I’m also looking for people to test brokers and provide feedback on any issues they encounter.

comments.author: MountainFancy1352
comments.body: Good luck about trading from the app. After I spent over 6 months building, backtesting and (sort of) paper trading, I just gave up on that part. I was using IBKR API for some of the data and paper account, all in a Hetzner server, most of the data came from Massive paid account, coding done on Cursor and VC with Claude Fable for assintance, and Grok/ CGPT doing daily continuous adversarial code reviews, on Anthropic max account, etc.etc. The worst part was finding bugs after months and months of running or Fable telling me months later that some of the backtests were not valid because of xyz. There is no way in hell I will put any real funds in an AI run account, not on trades run by the executioner. Don't get me wrong, the dashboard, graphics, statistics, conversations, planning, scanners, trade candidates, etc. etc. were all amazing and I'm proud of the accomplishment and learning exercise, but the reality is: it does not beat the SPY in the real world and some of the latest bugs I found tells me it would not be wise to fund the system on a live account with real money. I continue to work on new strategies and screeners  and different options for finding a better edge, but the trades will be done manually by yours truly, always. So, I do wish you good luck with the execution part

replies.author: OpenTraderWorld
replies.body:
I’ve been building bots for several years now, since before AI was widely available. And ever since AI became accessible, I’ve never delegated execution to it.  
I use AI for research, development, testing, orchestration, and, most importantly, to save a huge amount of time.  
My data comes from IBKR (paid). Buy/sell execution is first tested through simulated scenarios, then moved to paper trading, and finally to live trading once the behavior is considered reliable.  
As for outperforming the SPY, the amount of time invested, expertise, and luck all play a significant role.  
And yes, real trade execution is the most critical part of this project, which is precisely why it is intentionally being deployed last.

replies.author: Syneptic
replies.body: No offense but the way you write and talk makes you seem like you know nothing of this whole topic…

replies.author: MountainFancy1352
replies.body: Yes it is a lot of fun building all those working strategies in the apps with nice shiny dashboards, but if it doesn't beat the SPY, it is nothing more than a learning exercise, albeit a good one. The part that was really useful ( I am not formally qualified/competent) was to do continuous adversarial reviews by agents that have that specific role, and I do mean adversarial: pointing out the architectural mistakes, sequencing, and testing is something of great value in my opinion, also, historical data including delisted stocks is not cheap, this is where many systems fail and it is good to know before spending months chasing a wild goose

comments.author: CODE_HEIST
comments.body:
before adding execution, can the agent that edits a strategy also change its permissions? i'd want those to be separate, with a human confirming any increase in access.



i'm building TrenchersAI, so that boundary interests me more than another indicator. could you show a test where an agent tries an action outside its allowed scope?

replies.author: OpenTraderWorld
replies.body:
Permissions are scoped per module through the token: read-only, read/write, or full access. An agent can only access what its token explicitly grants.  
Broker connections are also currently read-only by design — there is no route that can place, modify, or cancel an order. Execution will be introduced separately, with its own credentials and permissions, so editing a strategy will not implicitly grant execution rights or allow the agent to elevate its own access.  
And yes, testing attempts outside the granted scope is part of what I want to validate before execution is enabled.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Nice project, and local-first with an MCP server is a good fit for research. I like that the backtest screen shows buy and hold next to the strategy result (20.47% vs 52.31% in your example) along with fees and expectancy per trade, since that's the honest comparison. For fundamentals, I'd trust sources that keep filing dates and restatements as separate versions, so backtests don't use numbers that weren't public yet. Cymetica's EventTrader is one example of event data (earnings, macro releases) built around that point-in-time timing, which could pair well with your calendar module.
